claim: Nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates (N-BPs) are a class of drugs widely prescribed to treat osteoporosis and other bone-related diseases.
source: Nitrogen-containing-bisphosphonates (N-BPs) are a class of drugs widely prescribed to treat osteoporosis and other bone-related diseases.
evidence: This is established knowledge about N-BPs and their clinical use.

claim: N-BPs function by inhibiting the mevalonate pathway in osteoclasts.
source: Although previous studies have established that N-BPs function by inhibiting the mevalonate pathway in osteoclasts, the mechanism by which N-BPs enter the cytosol from the extracellular space to reach their molecular target is not understood.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous studies.

claim: The mechanism by which N-BPs enter the cytosol from the extracellular space to reach their molecular target is not understood.
source: Although previous studies have established that N-BPs function by inhibiting the mevalonate pathway in osteoclasts, the mechanism by which N-BPs enter the cytosol from the extracellular space to reach their molecular target is not understood.
evidence: This represents a knowledge gap that the study aims to address.

claim: SLC37A3 is a gene required for the action of N-BPs in mammalian cells.
source: Here, we implemented a CRISPRi-mediated genome-wide screen and identified SLC37A3 (solute carrier family 37 member A3) as a gene required for the action of N-BPs in mammalian cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by the CRISPRi screen data presented in the manuscript.

claim: SLC37A3 forms a complex with ATRAID.
source: We observed that SLC37A3 forms a complex with ATRAID (all-trans retinoic acid-induced differentiation factor), a previously identified genetic target of N-BPs.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: SLC37A3 and ATRAID localize to lysosomes.
source: SLC37A3 and ATRAID localize to lysosomes and are required for releasing N-BP molecules that have trafficked to lysosomes through fluid-phase endocytosis into the cytosol.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3.

claim: SLC37A3 and ATRAID are required for releasing N-BP molecules that have trafficked to lysosomes through fluid-phase endocytosis into the cytosol.
source: SLC37A3 and ATRAID localize to lysosomes and are required for releasing N-BP molecules that have trafficked to lysosomes through fluid-phase endocytosis into the cytosol.
evidence: This is supported by radioactive uptake assays shown in Figure 4.

claim: N-BPs are the most commonly prescribed drugs used to treat osteoporosis.
source: N-BPs are the most commonly prescribed drugs used to treat osteoporosis (Drake et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Drake et al., 2008.

claim: N-BPs have two negatively charged phosphonate groups that bind to hydroxyapatite crystals with high affinity.
source: They have two negatively charged phosphonate groups that bind to hydroxyapatite crystals with high affinity and enable efficient accumulation of N-BPs on the bone surface (Drake et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Drake et al., 2008.

claim: The two negatively charged phosphonate groups enable efficient accumulation of N-BPs on the bone surface.
source: They have two negatively charged phosphonate groups that bind to hydroxyapatite crystals with high affinity and enable efficient accumulation of N-BPs on the bone surface (Drake et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Drake et al., 2008.

claim: Osteoclasts are the major cell type responsible for bone resorption.
source: Osteoclasts, the major cell type responsible for bone resorption, release N-BPs from the bone matrix by dissolving bone mineral and then take up N-BPs through fluid-phase endocytosis (Drake et al., 2008; Thompson et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge about osteoclast function.

claim: Osteoclasts release N-BPs from the bone matrix by dissolving bone mineral.
source: Osteoclasts, the major cell type responsible for bone resorption, release N-BPs from the bone matrix by dissolving bone mineral and then take up N-BPs through fluid-phase endocytosis (Drake et al., 2008; Thompson et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Drake et al., 2008 and Thompson et al., 2006.

claim: Osteoclasts take up N-BPs through fluid-phase endocytosis.
source: Osteoclasts, the major cell type responsible for bone resorption, release N-BPs from the bone matrix by dissolving bone mineral and then take up N-BPs through fluid-phase endocytosis (Drake et al., 2008; Thompson et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Drake et al., 2008 and Thompson et al., 2006.

claim: N-BPs inhibit farnesyl diphosphate synthase (FDPS) in the mevalonate pathway.
source: N-BPs subsequently inhibit farnesyl diphosphate synthase (FDPS) in the mevalonate pathway and reduce protein prenylation, an essential post-translational lipid modification required for the function of numerous proteins such as Ras, Rab and Rho, thereby inducing apoptosis in osteoclasts and diminishing their bone-resorption activities (Drake et al., 2008; Dunford et al., 2001; Fisher et al., 2000; Hughes et al., 1995; Kavanagh et al., 2006; Luckman et al., 1998a; Luckman et al., 1998b; van Beek et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: N-BPs reduce protein prenylation.
source: N-BPs subsequently inhibit farnesyl diphosphate synthase (FDPS) in the mevalonate pathway and reduce protein prenylation, an essential post-translational lipid modification required for the function of numerous proteins such as Ras, Rab and Rho, thereby inducing apoptosis in osteoclasts and diminishing their bone-resorption activities (Drake et al., 2008; Dunford et al., 2001; Fisher et al., 2000; Hughes et al., 1995; Kavanagh et al., 2006; Luckman et al., 1998a; Luckman et al., 1998b; van Beek et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Protein prenylation is an essential post-translational lipid modification required for the function of numerous proteins such as Ras, Rab and Rho.
source: N-BPs subsequently inhibit farnesyl diphosphate synthase (FDPS) in the mevalonate pathway and reduce protein prenylation, an essential post-translational lipid modification required for the function of numerous proteins such as Ras, Rab and Rho, thereby inducing apoptosis in osteoclasts and diminishing their bone-resorption activities (Drake et al., 2008; Dunford et al., 2001; Fisher et al., 2000; Hughes et al., 1995; Kavanagh et al., 2006; Luckman et al., 1998a; Luckman et al., 1998b; van Beek et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge about protein prenylation.

claim: N-BPs induce apoptosis in osteoclasts.
source: N-BPs subsequently inhibit farnesyl diphosphate synthase (FDPS) in the mevalonate pathway and reduce protein prenylation, an essential post-translational lipid modification required for the function of numerous proteins such as Ras, Rab and Rho, thereby inducing apoptosis in osteoclasts and diminishing their bone-resorption activities (Drake et al., 2008; Dunford et al., 2001; Fisher et al., 2000; Hughes et al., 1995; Kavanagh et al., 2006; Luckman et al., 1998a; Luckman et al., 1998b; van Beek et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: N-BPs diminish bone-resorption activities of osteoclasts.
source: N-BPs subsequently inhibit farnesyl diphosphate synthase (FDPS) in the mevalonate pathway and reduce protein prenylation, an essential post-translational lipid modification required for the function of numerous proteins such as Ras, Rab and Rho, thereby inducing apoptosis in osteoclasts and diminishing their bone-resorption activities (Drake et al., 2008; Dunford et al., 2001; Fisher et al., 2000; Hughes et al., 1995; Kavanagh et al., 2006; Luckman et al., 1998a; Luckman et al., 1998b; van Beek et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: FDPS is localized to the cytosol and peroxisomes.
source: However, it is not known how highly charged N-BPs exit the endocytic pathway to target FDPS, which is localized to the cytosol and peroxisomes (Martín et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Martín et al., 2007.

claim: It has been proposed that the acidification of endocytic compartments might neutralize the negative charges on the phosphonate groups and allow N-BPs to diffuse across the vesicle membrane.
source: It has been proposed that the acidification of endocytic compartments might neutralize the negative charges on the phosphonate groups and allow N-BPs to diffuse across the vesicle membrane (Thompson et al., 2006), but this model does not address the issue that the amine groups in N-BPs become positively charged in acidic environments.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from Thompson et al., 2006.

claim: The acidification model does not address the issue that the amine groups in N-BPs become positively charged in acidic environments.
source: It has been proposed that the acidification of endocytic compartments might neutralize the negative charges on the phosphonate groups and allow N-BPs to diffuse across the vesicle membrane (Thompson et al., 2006), but this model does not address the issue that the amine groups in N-BPs become positively charged in acidic environments.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on chemical properties of N-BPs.

claim: An alternative model is that a transporter exists that facilitates the exit of N-BPs from endocytic vesicles.
source: An alternative model is that a transporter exists that facilitates the exit of N-BPs from endocytic vesicles.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: The IC50 of alendronate in K562 cells is 250 μM.
source: The IC50 of alendronate in K562 cells is 250 μM.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 caption and can be inferred from Figure 1A.

claim: Enzymes, co-factors, and regulators of the mevalonate pathway are enriched in top hits from the CRISPRi screen.
source: Consistent with the current model for the action of N-BPs, enzymes, co-factors, and regulators of the mevalonate pathway are enriched in top hits (Figure 1C–D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by the screen data shown in Figure 1C-D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: Silencing of FDPS and GGPPS1 strongly sensitized cells to ALN.
source: Particularly, in accordance with the model that N-BPs induce cell death through inhibiting the enzymatic activities of FDPS and GGPPS1 (Drake et al., 2008), silencing of FDPS and GGPPS1 strongly sensitized cells to ALN (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by the screen data shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: Silencing of numerous enzymes in the pathway upstream of FDPS conferred strong resistance to ALN.
source: However, in contradiction with the current model of N-BP action, we observed that silencing of numerous enzymes in the pathway upstream of FDPS in fact conferred strong resistance to ALN (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the screen data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Inhibition of enzymes upstream of FDPS protects cells from ALN by preventing ALN-induced accumulation of IPP.
source: That work demonstrated that isopentenyl-5-pyrophosphate (IPP), the substrate of FDPS, is a toxic intermediate that interferes with DNA synthesis and causes DNA damage, suggesting that inhibition of enzymes upstream of FDPS protects cells from ALN by preventing ALN-induced accumulation of IPP.
evidence: This is based on inference from unpublished work by Horlbeck et al.

claim: IPP is a toxic intermediate that interferes with DNA synthesis and causes DNA damage.
source: That work demonstrated that isopentenyl-5-pyrophosphate (IPP), the substrate of FDPS, is a toxic intermediate that interferes with DNA synthesis and causes DNA damage, suggesting that inhibition of enzymes upstream of FDPS protects cells from ALN by preventing ALN-induced accumulation of IPP.
evidence: This is from unpublished work by Horlbeck et al.

claim: SLC37A3 conferred the strongest resistance amongst the resistance hits not known to be involved in the mevalonate pathway.
source: Amongst the resistance hits not known to be involved in the mevalonate pathway, the gene that conferred the strongest resistance was SLC37A3 (Figure 1C), which is predicted to encode a membrane protein with 12 transmembrane segments (Chou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the screen data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: SLC37A3 is predicted to encode a membrane protein with 12 transmembrane segments.
source: Amongst the resistance hits not known to be involved in the mevalonate pathway, the gene that conferred the strongest resistance was SLC37A3 (Figure 1C), which is predicted to encode a membrane protein with 12 transmembrane segments (Chou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chou et al., 2013.

claim: SLC37A3 appeared as a top resistance hit in a second CRISPRi screen using zoledronate.
source: SLC37A3 also appeared as a top resistance hit in a second CRISPRi screen using zoledronate, another representative N-BP, as the selection agent (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and Supplementary file 2), further supporting its role in the mechanism of action of N-BPs.
evidence: This is supported by the screen data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: SLC37A3 is predicted based on sequence homology to be a glucose-6-phosphate/phosphate antiporter.
source: SLC37A3 is predicted based on sequence homology to be a glucose-6-phosphate/phosphate antiporter (Chou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chou et al., 2013.

claim: SLC37A3 lacks glucose-6-phosphate/phosphate antiporter activity.
source: However, it has been demonstrated that SLC37A3 in fact lacks this predicted activity (Pan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pan et al., 2011.

claim: The physiological function of SLC37A3 has remained elusive.
source: To the best of our knowledge, the physiological function of SLC37A3 has remained elusive.
evidence: This represents a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: A human protein interactome study reported an interaction between SLC37A3 and ATRAID.
source: Intriguingly, a recent human protein interactome study reported an interaction between SLC37A3 and ATRAID (Huttlin et al., 2017), a type I transmembrane protein that was identified as an N-BP target in a previous work (Surface et al., unpublished) and our zoledronate CRISPRi screen (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), suggesting SLC37A3 and ATRAID might be functionally related.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Huttlin et al., 2017.

claim: ATRAID is a type I transmembrane protein.
source: Intriguingly, a recent human protein interactome study reported an interaction between SLC37A3 and ATRAID (Huttlin et al., 2017), a type I transmembrane protein that was identified as an N-BP target in a previous work (Surface et al., unpublished) and our zoledronate CRISPRi screen (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), suggesting SLC37A3 and ATRAID might be functionally related.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ATRAID structure.

claim: ATRAID was identified as an N-BP target in a previous work.
source: Intriguingly, a recent human protein interactome study reported an interaction between SLC37A3 and ATRAID (Huttlin et al., 2017), a type I transmembrane protein that was identified as an N-BP target in a previous work (Surface et al., unpublished) and our zoledronate CRISPRi screen (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), suggesting SLC37A3 and ATRAID might be functionally related.
evidence: This is supported by citation to unpublished work by Surface et al.

claim: ATRAID was identified in the zoledronate CRISPRi screen.
source: Intriguingly, a recent human protein interactome study reported an interaction between SLC37A3 and ATRAID (Huttlin et al., 2017), a type I transmembrane protein that was identified as an N-BP target in a previous work (Surface et al., unpublished) and our zoledronate CRISPRi screen (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), suggesting SLC37A3 and ATRAID might be functionally related.
evidence: This is supported by the screen data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Knockout of SLC37A3 and ATRAID in K562, HEK 293T, and RAW 264.7 cells conferred resistance to ALN.
source: Consistent with the CRISPRi screen and our previous results, knockout of SLC37A3 and ATRAID in all cell types conferred resistance to ALN (Figure 2A–C) (Surface et al., unpublished).
evidence: This is supported by the dose response data shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: Mature osteoclasts differentiated from knockout RAW cells are more resistant to ALN compared to those differentiated from wild-type cells.
source: Similarly, mature osteoclasts differentiated from knockout RAW cells are more resistant to ALN compared to those differentiated from wild-type cells (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) (Surface et al., unpublished).
evidence: This is supported by the dose response data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: ALN treatment had significantly less of an effect on protein prenylation in SLC37A3KO and ATRAIDKO cells compared to wild-type cells.
source: We also measured the reduction in protein prenylation as a readout of N-BP toxicity and verified that ALN treatment had significantly less of an effect on protein prenylation in SLC37A3KO and ATRAIDKO cells compared to wild-type cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by the immunoblot data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Complementation with epitope-tagged SLC37A3 in SLC37A3KO HEK 293T cells restored sensitivity to ALN.
source: Complementation with epitope-tagged SLC37A3 or either isoform of ATRAID (a short isoform, UniProt Q6UW56-1, and a long isoform, UniProt Q6UW56-3) in SLC37A3KO or ATRAIDKO HEK 293 T cells, respectively, restored sensitivity to ALN (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–D), confirming that the resistance to ALN observed in the knockout cells is indeed caused by the lack of SLC37A3 or ATRAID expression, and that the epitope-tagged versions of the two proteins are functional.
evidence: This is supported by the complementation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B-D.

claim: Complementation with either isoform of ATRAID in ATRAIDKO HEK 293T cells restored sensitivity to ALN.
source: Complementation with epitope-tagged SLC37A3 or either isoform of ATRAID (a short isoform, UniProt Q6UW56-1, and a long isoform, UniProt Q6UW56-3) in SLC37A3KO or ATRAIDKO HEK 293 T cells, respectively, restored sensitivity to ALN (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–D), confirming that the resistance to ALN observed in the knockout cells is indeed caused by the lack of SLC37A3 or ATRAID expression, and that the epitope-tagged versions of the two proteins are functional.
evidence: This is supported by the complementation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B-D.

claim: The epitope-tagged versions of SLC37A3 and ATRAID are functional.
source: Complementation with epitope-tagged SLC37A3 or either isoform of ATRAID (a short isoform, UniProt Q6UW56-1, and a long isoform, UniProt Q6UW56-3) in SLC37A3KO or ATRAIDKO HEK 293 T cells, respectively, restored sensitivity to ALN (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–D), confirming that the resistance to ALN observed in the knockout cells is indeed caused by the lack of SLC37A3 or ATRAID expression, and that the epitope-tagged versions of the two proteins are functional.
evidence: This is inferred from the complementation data showing restored sensitivity to ALN.

claim: SLC37A3KO cells are more resistant to ALN compared to ATRAIDKO cells.
source: We observed that SLC37A3KO cells are more resistant to ALN compared to ATRAIDKO cells, and the knockout of ATRAID in addition to SLC37A3 did not further protect cells from the drug (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2J), indicating that ATRAID and SLC37A3 are indeed functionally related and that SLC37A3 is epistatic to ATRAID.
evidence: This is supported by the dose response data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2J.

claim: The knockout of ATRAID in addition to SLC37A3 did not further protect cells from ALN.
source: We observed that SLC37A3KO cells are more resistant to ALN compared to ATRAIDKO cells, and the knockout of ATRAID in addition to SLC37A3 did not further protect cells from the drug (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2J), indicating that ATRAID and SLC37A3 are indeed functionally related and that SLC37A3 is epistatic to ATRAID.
evidence: This is supported by the dose response data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2J.

claim: ATRAID and SLC37A3 are functionally related.
source: We observed that SLC37A3KO cells are more resistant to ALN compared to ATRAIDKO cells, and the knockout of ATRAID in addition to SLC37A3 did not further protect cells from the drug (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2J), indicating that ATRAID and SLC37A3 are indeed functionally related and that SLC37A3 is epistatic to ATRAID.
evidence: This is inferred from the epistasis data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2J.

claim: SLC37A3 is epistatic to ATRAID.
source: We observed that SLC37A3KO cells are more resistant to ALN compared to ATRAIDKO cells, and the knockout of ATRAID in addition to SLC37A3 did not further protect cells from the drug (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2J), indicating that ATRAID and SLC37A3 are indeed functionally related and that SLC37A3 is epistatic to ATRAID.
evidence: This is inferred from the epistasis data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2J.

claim: Epitope-tagged SLC37A3 and ATRAID are not over-expressed.
source: We confirmed that epitope-tagged SLC37A3 and ATRAID are not over-expressed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the expression data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: SLC37A3 co-localizes with LAMP2, a lysosomal marker.
source: We observed that SLC37A3 co-localizes with LAMP2, a lysosomal marker, but not with Na+/K+-ATPase or EEA1, which mark the plasma membrane and early endosomes, respectively (Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A-B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: SLC37A3 does not co-localize with Na+/K+-ATPase or EEA1.
source: We observed that SLC37A3 co-localizes with LAMP2, a lysosomal marker, but not with Na+/K+-ATPase or EEA1, which mark the plasma membrane and early endosomes, respectively (Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A-B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Both isoforms of ATRAID predominantly localize to lysosomes.
source: Consistent with a previous report (Ding et al., 2015), both isoforms of ATRAID also predominantly localize to lysosomes but not to the plasma membrane or early endosomes (Figure 3C–D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,F–H).
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3C-D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,F-H, and is consistent with Ding et al., 2015.

claim: Both isoforms of ATRAID predominantly co-localize with SLC37A3.
source: When we co-expressed functional and epitope-tagged SLC37A3 and ATRAID (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B), we observed that both isoforms of ATRAID predominantly co-localize with SLC37A3 (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: SLC37A3 and ATRAID physically interact.
source: To investigate whether the observed co-localization between SLC37A3 and ATRAID represents a physical interaction, we performed reciprocal co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) experiments in HEK 293 T cells over-expressing the two proteins. We detected an interaction between SLC37A3 and ATRAID in both pull-down directions (Figure 3F), confirming that SLC37A3 and ATRAID physically interact, likely forming a lysosomal complex.
evidence: This is supported by the co-IP data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: SLC37A3 and ATRAID likely form a lysosomal complex.
source: To investigate whether the observed co-localization between SLC37A3 and ATRAID represents a physical interaction, we performed reciprocal co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) experiments in HEK 293 T cells over-expressing the two proteins. We detected an interaction between SLC37A3 and ATRAID in both pull-down directions (Figure 3F), confirming that SLC37A3 and ATRAID physically interact, likely forming a lysosomal complex.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-IP data and localization data.

claim: Deletion of ATRAID significantly reduces the protein level of SLC37A3.
source: As it has been reported that the expression levels of certain solute carriers depend on the presence of accessory proteins (Makrides et al., 2014), we investigated the possibility that the functional relationship between ATRAID and SLC37A3 is due to the impaired expression of SLC37A3 in the absence of ATRAID. Indeed, when we expressed SLC37A3 in the KO2 cells, we observed a substantial decrease in the protein level of SLC37A3 compared to that when expressed in the SLC37A3KO background (Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), even though the mRNA levels of SLC37A3 in both backgrounds are similar (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the immunoblot data shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The mRNA levels of SLC37A3 in SLC37A3KO and KO2 backgrounds are similar.
source: Indeed, when we expressed SLC37A3 in the KO2 cells, we observed a substantial decrease in the protein level of SLC37A3 compared to that when expressed in the SLC37A3KO background (Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), even though the mRNA levels of SLC37A3 in both backgrounds are similar (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The protein level of SLC37A3 was restored by complementation with either isoform of ATRAID.
source: The protein level of SLC37A3 was restored by complementation with either isoform of ATRAID (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by the immunoblot data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Reduced protein levels of both isoforms of ATRAID were observed in the KO2 background.
source: In reciprocity, we also observed reduced protein levels of both isoforms of ATRAID in the KO2 background that cannot be explained by changes in transcript levels (Figure 3H, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the immunoblot data shown in Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B-C.

claim: The translation efficiency of SLC37A3 transcripts is not significantly altered in the absence of ATRAID.
source: As the translation efficiency of SLC37A3 transcripts is not significantly altered in the absence of ATRAID (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–E), the decreased SLC37A3 protein level in the KO2 background is likely caused by shortened protein half-life, suggesting that ATRAID and SLC37A3 are mutually dependent for their stability.
evidence: This is supported by the polysome profiling data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D-E.

claim: The decreased SLC37A3 protein level in the KO2 background is likely caused by shortened protein half-life.
source: As the translation efficiency of SLC37A3 transcripts is not significantly altered in the absence of ATRAID (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–E), the decreased SLC37A3 protein level in the KO2 background is likely caused by shortened protein half-life, suggesting that ATRAID and SLC37A3 are mutually dependent for their stability.
evidence: This is inferred from the translation efficiency and protein level data.

claim: ATRAID and SLC37A3 are mutually dependent for their stability.
source: As the translation efficiency of SLC37A3 transcripts is not significantly altered in the absence of ATRAID (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–E), the decreased SLC37A3 protein level in the KO2 background is likely caused by shortened protein half-life, suggesting that ATRAID and SLC37A3 are mutually dependent for their stability.
evidence: This is inferred from the protein stability data.

claim: The deletion of ATRAID altered the glycosylation pattern of SLC37A3.
source: Intriguingly, the deletion of ATRAID also altered the glycosylation pattern of SLC37A3. In the absence of ATRAID, the mature, glycosylated population of SLC37A3 (around 50kD) became undetectable, whereas a population of un-glycosylated SLC37A3 (around 40kD) emerged (Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is supported by the immunoblot data shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 2F.

claim: In the absence of ATRAID, the mature, glycosylated population of SLC37A3 became undetectable.
source: Intriguingly, the deletion of ATRAID also altered the glycosylation pattern of SLC37A3. In the absence of ATRAID, the mature, glycosylated population of SLC37A3 (around 50kD) became undetectable, whereas a population of un-glycosylated SLC37A3 (around 40kD) emerged (Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is supported by the immunoblot data shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Only the glycosylated population of SLC37A3 interacted with ATRAID.
source: Moreover, in cells overexpressing SLC37A3, although a significant proportion of SLC37A3 remained un-glycosylated, only the glycosylated population of SLC37A3 interacted with ATRAID (Figure 3—figure supplement 2G), suggesting that the interaction with ATRAID is crucial for the expression of correctly modified SLC37A3.
evidence: This is supported by the co-IP data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2G.

claim: The interaction with ATRAID is crucial for the expression of correctly modified SLC37A3.
source: Moreover, in cells overexpressing SLC37A3, although a significant proportion of SLC37A3 remained un-glycosylated, only the glycosylated population of SLC37A3 interacted with ATRAID (Figure 3—figure supplement 2G), suggesting that the interaction with ATRAID is crucial for the expression of correctly modified SLC37A3.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-IP data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2G.

claim: SLC37A3 resides on the membrane of vesicles in which internalized fluorescently-labeled zoledronate accumulates.
source: Given the predicted function of SLC37A3 as a transporter, we hypothesized that ATRAID and SLC37A3 transport N-BP molecules across the lipid bilayer to inhibit FDPS. Indeed, we observed that SLC37A3 resides on the membrane of vesicles in which internalized fluorescently-labeled zoledronate (AF647-ZLN) accumulates (Figure 4A), supporting its role as a transporter of N-BPs.
evidence: This is supported by the live cell imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There was no significant difference in whole-cell accumulation of radioactivity between the knockouts and wild-type cells when incubated with radioactive ALN.
source: When we incubated wild-type, ATRAIDKO and SLC37A3KO cells with radioactive ALN (3H-ALN) and measured total intracellular radioactivity, we observed no significant difference in whole-cell accumulation of radioactivity between the knockouts and wild-type cells (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by the radioactive uptake assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The distribution of radioactive signal changed from being primarily in the cytosolic fraction in wild-type cells to being predominantly in membranous fractions in SLC37A3KO and ATRAIDKO cells.
source: We observed that the distribution of radioactive signal changed from being primarily in the cytosolic fraction in wild-type cells to being predominantly in membranous fractions in SLC37A3KO and ATRAIDKO cells (Figure 4C), suggesting that 3H-ALN cannot be released from membrane-bound organelles in knockout cells.
evidence: This is supported by the fractionation-based radioactive uptake assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: 3H-ALN cannot be released from membrane-bound organelles in knockout cells.
source: We observed that the distribution of radioactive signal changed from being primarily in the cytosolic fraction in wild-type cells to being predominantly in membranous fractions in SLC37A3KO and ATRAIDKO cells (Figure 4C), suggesting that 3H-ALN cannot be released from membrane-bound organelles in knockout cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the fractionation-based radioactive uptake assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: There was a significant enrichment of 3H-ALN in lysosomes purified from knockout cells compared to those from wild-type cells.
source: As our model predicted, we observed a significant enrichment of 3H-ALN in lysosomes purified from knockout cells compared to those from wild-type cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by the lysosome purification-based radioactive uptake assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: ATRAIDKO cells phenocopied SLC37A3KO cells in radioactive uptake assays.
source: Additionally, consistent with the observation that ATRAID is required for the stable expression of SLC37A3, ATRAIDKO cells phenocopied SLC37A3KO cells in these uptake assays.
evidence: This is inferred from the radioactive uptake assay data shown in Figure 4.

claim: N-BPs traffic to lysosomes after internalization through endocytosis.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that N-BPs traffic to lysosomes after internalization through endocytosis, and SLC37A3 and ATRAID form a lysosomal transporter complex that releases N-BP molecules from the lumen of lysosomes into the cytosol.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data on localization and radioactive uptake assays.

claim: SLC37A3 and ATRAID form a lysosomal transporter complex that releases N-BP molecules from the lumen of lysosomes into the cytosol.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that N-BPs traffic to lysosomes after internalization through endocytosis, and SLC37A3 and ATRAID form a lysosomal transporter complex that releases N-BP molecules from the lumen of lysosomes into the cytosol.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data on localization, co-IP, and radioactive uptake assays.

claim: A recent study has proposed that patients who harbor a genetic variant of GGPS1 might be more prone to the side-effects of N-BP treatment.
source: As a recent study has proposed that patients who harbor a genetic variant of GGPS1 might be more prone to the side-effects of N-BP treatment (Roca-Ayats et al., 2017), it is possible that patients with variants of SLC37A3 or ATRAID, which are genes crucial for the action of N-BPs, might also exhibit non-canonical responsiveness to the drugs.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Roca-Ayats et al., 2017.

claim: Patients with variants of SLC37A3 or ATRAID might exhibit non-canonical responsiveness to N-BPs.
source: As a recent study has proposed that patients who harbor a genetic variant of GGPS1 might be more prone to the side-effects of N-BP treatment (Roca-Ayats et al., 2017), it is possible that patients with variants of SLC37A3 or ATRAID, which are genes crucial for the action of N-BPs, might also exhibit non-canonical responsiveness to the drugs.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings of the study and previous work on GGPS1.

claim: The knockout cells are resistant to N-BPs other than ALN.
source: The knockout cells are also resistant to N-BPs other than ALN (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E) but not to non-nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates (non-N-BPs), which do not target FDPS (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F) (Drake et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by the dose response data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E.

claim: The knockout cells are not resistant to non-nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates.
source: The knockout cells are also resistant to N-BPs other than ALN (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E) but not to non-nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates (non-N-BPs), which do not target FDPS (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F) (Drake et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by the dose response data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Non-nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates do not target FDPS.
source: The knockout cells are also resistant to N-BPs other than ALN (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E) but not to non-nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates (non-N-BPs), which do not target FDPS (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F) (Drake et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Drake et al., 2008.

claim: Knockout of SLC37A3 and ATRAID did not protect cells from lovastatin.
source: Interestingly, knockout of SLC37A3 and ATRAID did not protect cells from lovastatin (LOV), a statin drug that also targets the mevalonate pathway (Figure 2—figure supplement 2G–I) (Tiwari and Khokhar, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the dose response data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2G-I.

claim: Lovastatin is a statin drug that targets the mevalonate pathway.
source: Interestingly, knockout of SLC37A3 and ATRAID did not protect cells from lovastatin (LOV), a statin drug that also targets the mevalonate pathway (Figure 2—figure supplement 2G–I) (Tiwari and Khokhar, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tiwari and Khokhar, 2014.

claim: The roles of SLC37A3 and ATRAID in the mechanism of action of N-BPs are not related to the mevalonate pathway but are instead specific to N-BPs.
source: The distinctive responses of SLC37A3KO and ATRAIDKO cells to N-BPs, non-N-BPs, and LOV indicate that the roles of SLC37A3 and ATRAID in the mechanism of action of N-BPs are not related to the mevalonate pathway but are instead specific to N-BPs.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential responses to different drugs shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E-I.
